d: Parts are not consistently grouped into families, product lines or clusters, so pricing rules cannot be applied at scale.

t: Value and volume segments not separated
d: There is no distinction between value-capture parts and high-volume cost-driven parts, so willingness to pay is left unrealised.
List, floor, target and peer reference points are undefined per segment, so there is no benchmark to price against or alert on.
Approval thresholds, dual-control rules and role-based rights are informal or held in spreadsheets rather than systematised.
Product, customer, region and channel hierarchies are incomplete or inconsistent, undermining every downstream pricing rule.

t: Volume tiers, pack sizes and MOQ unmanaged
d: Quantity-based price tiers, units of measure, pack sizes and minimum order quantities are not held as structured, reusable rules.

t: Strategy not translated into executable rules
d: Commercial strategy lives in presentations rather than machine-executable pricing rules, so intent and execution drift apart.
Customers cannot be linked into parent and subsidiary structures, so the same buying group is priced inconsistently across its entities.

t: New-part pricing is slow and manual
d: New parts wait in a queue for classification and a first price, delaying availability and leaving early revenue uncaptured.
The system cannot propose a price from rules, cost and market signals when some inputs are missing, so every new price is built by hand.
Cost-plus, mark-up, fixed-price, recommended-retail-minus and value-based methods cannot run together and be prioritised per cluster or channel.
Replacement and linked-part relationships are not maintained, so price carry-over and consistency for related parts is unreliable.
Large initial-price loads lack validation, a profit-impact preview and a rollback path, making mass uploads risky.

t: No margin simulation on new parts
d: The margin and volume impact of a first price cannot be simulated before it is approved and stored.
When a cost or other input is missing, the engine stops instead of bridging the gap to still propose a defensible price.
There is no model that translates internal and external drivers into a target margin per product line, nor a way to visualise the resulting margin curve.
The target margin cannot be adjusted for very high or very low-cost parts, distorting price points at the extremes of the range.
Value parts cannot be priced item by item from value attributes off a reference point, so value capture stays coarse and generic.

t: Bundle and kit pricing not built in
d: Kit, bundle and assembly prices cannot be calculated bottom-up from the latest component prices inside the tool.
When input or production cost moves, repricing is manual and lagging, eroding margin until someone notices.
Applying a scoped, differentiated percentage or absolute increase across families and segments with impact simulation is manual and error-prone.
The price, revenue and margin impact of a central adjustment cannot be simulated and saved before it is activated, so changes ship blind.
Component surcharges and import or export tariff elements cannot be tracked at component level and reflected into the central price build-up.
Inconsistencies such as variant or attribute mismatches are not flagged automatically during adjustment, so errors slip through.

t: Reporting does not point to action
d: Margin and volume reporting does not surface where central pricing action is needed, so adjustments stay reactive.

t: Channel cost and price moves not linked
d: Cost and price changes in one supply channel do not propagate to the related service channel, breaking price relationships.
Service-channel prices cannot be compared against independent-channel levels per part or customer to position competitively.
Releasing approved central prices and structures to markets is a manual transfer with no shared status or trail.
Markets do not automatically receive a list of what changed and what needs local processing.
Corridors, rules and approval limits do not flow with the price to the market level, so local steering loses its guardrails.

t: HQ and markets on disconnected systems
d: Headquarters and market levels run on separate pricing systems with no shared logic or data transparency.
Local price derivation from the central price and a market factor is not calculated automatically from rules and scoring.
Revisable rates and threshold-triggered recalculation when a rate move crosses a boundary are not handled cleanly.
Upper and lower factor corridors per segment, market or competition are not enforced, so local prices drift outside policy.
Market-specific limits on percentage price change, with lower and upper bounds per product line and customer, are applied inconsistently.

t: Local prices not checked against the market
d: Market list prices are not checked for consistency against observed competitive price levels in the same market.
Markets cannot simulate the local margin impact of a derived price before preparing it for approval.
Dealer prices off the market list price via multi-dimension discount structures are maintained by hand and drift quickly.
The margin and revenue impact of a local price change is not shown to the approver, so decisions are made without the number.
Local price-change approval and rationale capture runs on email and spreadsheets rather than a tracked, conditional workflow.
Local prices that fall below minimum-margin thresholds are not flagged automatically for corrective action.
Manually overridden local prices are not tracked, reviewed or automatically reverted when their validity expires.
Markets cannot iteratively simulate an increase to reach a margin or revenue target, with suggested moves to get there.
Local margin and volume performance cannot be analysed per segment or customer to shortlist the next pricing actions.
Tiered discount-approval bands are not enforced, so concessions routinely exceed the granter's authority.
Temporary prices lack scoped validity, minimum-margin checks and automatic revert once the campaign ends.

t: Special and regional price requests are clumsy
d: Distributor, importer and key-account price lists and regional requests are hard to capture and maintain with eligibility control.
The uplift effect of promotions is not measured, so spend on slow-moving and seasonal campaigns is not optimised.

t: Discount and rebate logic is fragmented
d: Discount and rebate models are not defined flexibly per segment or customer, so true net realisation is opaque.
Customer-specific discounts, dealer bonuses and target agreements are not managed as governed commercial conditions.
Long-term agreement scenarios that respect cost development and volume commitments cannot be modelled before signing.
There is no alerting before supply obligations or contract end dates lapse, risking compliance and supply gaps.

t: Bid and quotation process not supported
d: Bids cannot be monitored or informed by past bid history, so new quotations repeat earlier pricing mistakes.

t: Publication to core systems is fragile
d: Approved prices are not reliably published to ERP, logistics, product-information and invoicing systems with validated timing.
Prices cannot be distributed flexibly (full or delta lists, interfaces, future-dated) to every consuming system and customer format.
There is no clean separation of approval date, communication date and system-activation date for a price change.
Distributed prices are not confirmed as received and consistent by downstream systems, risking silent gaps.
Differences for the same part across markets and channels, and validity-date mismatches between systems, are not surfaced.
The who, what, when and why of each price change is not fully logged with a unique reference and retained for the required period.
A price point cannot be traced back to the rule, driver, cost and approval that produced it.
Role separation, the authorisation hierarchy and documented approvals do not meet audit or regulatory requirements.
Data retention and deletion obligations, including data-subject requests, are not enforced systematically.
Audit, compliance and price-health reporting is assembled by hand rather than generated from the pricing record itself.
